planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this extremely old Russian selection needs a compatible pollinizer and is valued foremost for its winter hardiness rather than keeping quality.

directions: Grushovka Moskovskaya is a centuries-old Russian summer apple first recorded in the late 1700s and still widely grown across the colder apple-growing regions of Russia for its outstanding cold tolerance. The small, rounded, pale yellow-green fruit is streaked and flushed with red, with juicy, tart-sweet white flesh that ripens in mid to late summer but drops quickly and stores for only a few weeks, so plan to use the crop fresh or process it into sauce and juice soon after picking. The tree bears heavily and at a young age, making it a dependable choice where many other apple cultivars suffer winter dieback. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect a vigorous, hardy tree needing only routine pruning to maintain an open canopy.
sources: N.I. Vavilov Institute of Plant Genetic Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall, setting the crown slightly below soil level to encourage new basal shoots; Selechenskaya is a Russian-bred black currant valued for very large, early-ripening fruit.

directions: Selechenskaya is a Russian black currant selection prized for unusually large, rounded berries that ripen early in the season and carry a sweeter, less acidic flavor than many European black currant cultivars. The upright, vigorous bush shows strong tolerance of extreme winter cold along with good resistance to powdery mildew and currant mite, making it a dependable choice in short-season northern gardens. Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, mulching well since the roots are shallow, and renewal-prune about a third of the oldest wood each dormant season since the heaviest fruiting occurs on one-year-old canes.
sources: N.I. Vavilov Institute of Plant Genetic Resources

common_name: Yadrenaya Black Currant (Siberian Giant Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Yadrenaya is a Siberian-bred black currant selected for exceptionally large fruit and extreme cold hardiness.

directions: Yadrenaya was bred in Siberia and is known among black currant growers for producing some of the largest berries in the species, with a brisk, tart flavor that holds up well after mid-late season ripening. The bush was selected under some of the harshest winter conditions any cultivated currant faces, so it tolerates extreme cold with ease and remains productive in short, cool growing seasons where many other fruiting shrubs struggle. Grow it in full sun in fertile, consistently moist soil, mulching to protect the shallow root system, and cut out the oldest one-third of canes each winter to keep the plant fruiting on vigorous young wood.
sources: N.I. Vavilov Institute of Plant Genetic Resources

common_name: Ukrainian Beet (Heritage Long Purple Borscht Beet)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; this heirloom was maintained for decades through UK and Ukrainian seed-saver networks specifically for its tender, easy-peeling roots.

directions: Ukrainian is a long-rooted heirloom beet grown across Ukraine and Eastern Europe primarily for borscht, where its deep red flesh and tender, easy-to-peel skin make it especially convenient for peeling in quantity. Sow seed directly in loose, stone-free soil as soon as it can be worked, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up without crowding. The flesh stays notably tender even as the root lengthens, making it equally good raw in salads or simmered into soup, and roots can be left in the ground longer than many round beet types before turning woody. Harvest once roots reach usable size and store the surplus in damp sand in a cool cellar for winter use.

planting.note: Start seedlings indoors or in a cold frame and transplant out 45-50 days later; Kharkov Winter is a long-season Ukrainian heirloom grown for cold tolerance and long storage rather than speed.

directions: Kharkov Winter is a late-maturing Ukrainian heirloom cabbage grown for dense, round-flat heads that can weigh seven to eleven pounds and resist splitting in the field. The thick, juicy leaves and strong cold tolerance make it a traditional choice for late-season harvest and long winter keeping, and it has long been favored for sauerkraut as well as fresh use. Transplant hardened-off seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving plants ample spacing to bulk up over their long growing season, and keep moisture consistent to prevent head cracking as cabbages approach maturity. Harvest once heads feel solid when pressed, and cure briefly before cool storage for winter use.
sources: Seed catalog archives, Eastern European heirloom vegetable collections

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this old Thurgau cider apple needs a compatible pollinizer and keeps remarkably well in storage.

directions: Uttwiler Spätlauber is a Swiss heirloom apple documented since about 1750 around Uttwil in the canton of Thurgau, grown chiefly for cider and kitchen use thanks to its sharp, acidic flavor. Fruit stays smooth, shiny green for most of the season, coloring only lightly yellow-green and sometimes blushed brownish-red where exposed to full sun, and the firm, crisp flesh resembles that of Golden Delicious. It reaches picking maturity relatively late, in mid-October, and the skin notably does not shrivel in storage, allowing fruit to keep in good condition for up to a year in a cool cellar. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer nearby, and prune to an open framework to let light reach the fruit.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this old Zurich-canton apple needs a compatible pollinizer and suits both juicing and the kitchen.

directions: Schneiderapfel is a Swiss heirloom apple that arose as a chance seedling in the canton of Zurich in 1746 and has remained popular for juicing and cooking ever since. The medium to large, rounded fruit shows a bright green base color blushed with pale red, and the pale yellow flesh is crisp, juicy, and well balanced between sweetness and acidity with a distinct aromatic character. It performs reliably across a range of Swiss growing sites and has long been a dependable dual-purpose choice where a single tree needs to supply both fresh eating and juice. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer, and prune annually to maintain an open, light-filled canopy for good fruit quality.

common_name: Berner Landfrauen Pole Bean (Bernese Farmwife Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; provide sturdy poles or a trellis at least 8 feet tall, as this vigorous Swiss heirloom climbs well beyond typical pole bean height.

directions: Berner Landfrauen, whose Swiss German name translates roughly to Bernese farmwife bean, is a heritage pole bean long cultivated and preserved by countrywomen in the Bern region of Switzerland. The round, stringless pods are green mottled with purple speckling, and the plant is dual-purpose, picked young as a snap bean or left to dry on the vine for shelling and baking. It is notably vigorous, climbing poles eight feet or taller, so set sturdy supports before sowing and expect a long, productive harvest window once pods begin forming about ten weeks after sowing. Grow in warm, fertile soil in full sun with consistent moisture, and pick snap pods regularly to keep the vines producing.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Schwerzi is a vigorous, undemanding Swiss perry and drying pear rather than a fresh dessert type.

directions: Schwerzi is a traditional Swiss pear found historically in the cantons of Aargau, Bern, Lucerne, and Zurich, grown on a fast-growing, large tree that tolerates a wide range of sites without much fuss. The small fruit has crisp, juicy flesh with a sharp, spicy sourness rather than mellow sweetness, and it does not keep long off the tree, lasting at most about ten days before use. Most of the harvest traditionally goes into pear cider, schnapps, and baking, or is sliced and air-dried into dörrbirnen, dried pear slices that develop crunchy sugar crystals around the core as they dry. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer, and give the tree plenty of room to reach its eventual large size.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste: Schwerzi Pear
